items.question: Assess the contribution of the Kakatiyas of Warangal to the polity, economy and culture of the Telugu country.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Kakatiyas (c. 1163–1323)**, ruling from **Orugallu (Warangal)**, were the first dynasty to weld the **upland Telangana and the deltaic coast into a single Telugu political and cultural unit**, and their legacy underpins Telugu identity to this day.

**Polity.** Rising from **feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and Western Chalukyas**, they asserted sovereignty under **Rudradeva in 1163** (Anumakonda inscription). Their most striking political innovation was the **nayankara/nayaka system** — a warrior-landholder status open to men of **any birth**, which recruited peasants into the army and created remarkable **social mobility**. **Ganapati Deva (1199–1262)** unified the Godavari–Krishna deltas, and **Rudrama Devi**, one of the very few **women sovereigns** of medieval India, defended the realm against the Yadavas — her rule winning the praise of **Marco Polo**.

**Economy.** The Kakatiyas transformed the dry uplands through a vast network of **irrigation 'tanks' (reservoirs)** — **Pakhal, Laknavaram and Ramappa Cheruvu** — many still functioning. They actively promoted commerce: Ganapati Deva's **Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam** guaranteed the **safety of foreign merchants** and charged only fixed low duties, making Motupalli a thriving port.

**Culture.** They patronised **Telugu**, replacing Kannada in inscriptions, and supported writers such as **Tikkana, Palkuriki Somanatha** and **Jayapa Senani** (Nrittaratnavali on dance). In architecture they created a distinctive style — the **Thousand Pillar Temple (Hanamkonda)**, **Warangal Fort** with the **Kakatiya Kala Thoranam** (now Telangana's emblem), and above all the **Ramappa Temple** (1213), whose floating bricks and sand-box foundation earned it **UNESCO World Heritage status in 2021**.

**Conclusion.** Though the dynasty fell to the Tughlaqs in 1323, its consolidation of Telugu-speaking territory, its egalitarian warrior order, its tank-irrigation economy and its temple art gave the Andhra region a durable cultural foundation that outlived the kingdom itself.
keyPoints: Kakatiyas (1163–1323), capital Orugallu/Warangal; first to unify upland Telangana with the coastal delta.
Nayankara/nayaka system opened warrior status to all births, enabling social mobility.
Ganapati Deva expanded to the Godavari–Krishna delta; Rudrama Devi was a rare woman sovereign praised by Marco Polo.
Economy built on irrigation tanks (Pakhal, Laknavaram) and trade via Motupalli's Abhaya Sasanam.
Cultural legacy: Telugu literary patronage; Thousand Pillar Temple, Warangal Fort/Kala Thoranam, Ramappa (UNESCO 2021).

items.question: Trace the circumstances of the fall of the Kakatiya kingdom and the nature of the Telugu resistance under the Musunuri Nayakas.
items.modelAnswer:
The fall of the Kakatiyas and the revival led by the **Musunuri Nayakas** together form the pivotal episode by which the Telugu country resisted and recovered from Delhi's expansion into the Deccan.

**The fall.** From the early 14th century the **Delhi Sultanate** repeatedly assailed **Prataparudra II** (r. 1289–1323). An early Khalji foray was thrown back at **Upparapalli (1303)**, but in **1310 Malik Kafur** besieged Orugallu and forced Prataparudra into **tribute** (the **Koh-i-Noor** reputedly passing to Delhi); a further siege in **1318** renewed his submission. Finally, in **1323**, **Ulugh Khan (Jauna Khan)**, son of **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**, took Warangal after a prolonged siege; Prataparudra was captured and is believed to have **died near the Narmada**. Orugallu was renamed **Sultanpur**, and the Telugu land descended into confusion under alien governors — a devastation vividly recorded in the Vilasa grant.

**The resistance.** Out of this chaos rose the **Musunuri Nayakas**, claiming **Kakatiya heritage**. **Prolaya Nayaka**, ruling from **Rekapalle near Bhadrachalam**, issued the **Vilasa copper-plate grant (c. 1330)**, presenting himself as the restorer of dharma and order. His cousin **Kapaya Nayaka (1333–1368)** organised a **confederacy of 75 Nayakas** and, with the aid of the Hoysala **Veera Ballala III**, **recovered Warangal from the Tughlaq governor Malik Maqbul in 1336** — a genuinely 'national' revolt that expelled Delhi's authority from Telangana. Kapaya assumed the title **'Andhra Suratrana'**.

**Aftermath.** Kapaya's position was gradually eroded by the rising **Bahmani Sultanate** (to whom he ceded Golconda) and by internal rivals; he was defeated and killed by the **Recherla Nayakas at Bhimavaram in 1368**. The resistance nonetheless kept the Telugu country out of Delhi's grip and paved the way for the **Reddi kingdoms and the Vijayanagara empire**.

**Conclusion.** The Kakatiyas fell to superior Sultanate arms, but the Musunuri interlude showed the resilience of Telugu political society, preserving its cultural continuity until new indigenous powers consolidated the region.
keyPoints: Prataparudra II faced sieges in 1303 (Upparapalli), 1310 (Malik Kafur, tribute), 1318 and 1323.
1323: Ulugh Khan under Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq conquered Warangal; Orugallu renamed Sultanpur.
Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka issued the Vilasa grant (c.1330) claiming Kakatiya heritage.
Kapaya Nayaka recovered Warangal in 1336 with 75 Nayakas and Hoysala Veera Ballala III's help; took the title 'Andhra Suratrana'.
Kapaya lost ground to the Bahmanis and was killed by the Recherla Nayakas in 1368, opening the way for the Reddis and Vijayanagara.
